transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, thank you. It's... it's a bit hard to pinpoint exactly when things started feeling off, because in my line of work—I'm a healthcare social worker, so I'm constantly dealing with other people's crises and discharging patients—you get so used to just pushing through and ignoring your own needs. But what finally made me realize I needed to come in, what actually made me pick up the phone and make this appointment, is that my appetite has just been completely all over the place for months now. 

It's just so unpredictable. There will be these long stretches where I just skip dinner entirely. I'll get home from work, walk through the door, and I just can't bring myself to eat a single thing. I've actually been losing weight without even trying to... which I know some people might think sounds like a good thing, but it really just doesn't feel right to me. And then on the other nights, instead of skipping a meal completely, I just sort of stand in the kitchen and pick at things. I'll have a handful of saltine crackers, or I'll just eat some cereal straight out of the box, just because the entire concept of actually cooking a meal for myself feels so incredibly pointless. The thought of getting out a pan, or chopping vegetables, or even just turning on the stove... it just feels like, what is the point? It's too much effort when I have absolutely zero desire to eat anyway. I just don't know why my relationship with food has gotten so entirely derailed like this, but it's been months of this back-and-forth and I just can't seem to get back to normal.
Have you been feeling sad or down most of the time lately?

Sad? You know, it's funny you ask it that way, because... well, no, I wouldn't say I feel sad, exactly. I mean, working in healthcare, I see profound sadness every single day. I see families getting terrible news, I see people crying in the hallways, dealing with unimaginable grief... that's sadness. I don't feel like that. I'm not sitting at home weeping or feeling heartbroken or anything. 

It’s more just... I don't know. I don't feel "down in the dumps" in that classic way people talk about when they picture someone who is struggling. I actually was just telling my sister on the phone last weekend—she asked me almost the exact same thing because she was worried about me—and I told her, "I'm not sad!" It's just... well, I don't know how to describe it other than just feeling completely blank. But no, crying or feeling gloomy or down? Not really. I just feel like I'm going through the motions, I guess, but without the actual emotion of sadness attached to it, if that makes any sense at all. It's so hard to explain because everyone expects you to say you're crying all the time when things feel wrong, but that's just not what's happening with me. I'm just... not sad.
Do you find yourself enjoying activities that you used to like?

Enjoying things? Well, that's another thing that's just... it's just so frustrating lately. I mean, I still try. I really do. I still go through the motions of doing the things I used to absolutely love. Like my garden, for instance. I have this beautiful perennial garden in the backyard that I've spent years cultivating—hostas, daylilies, some really lovely hydrangeas—and I used to spend hours out there every weekend. I'd lose track of time just weeding and pruning. Now, I still go out there to water it, because I can't stand the thought of everything dying on my watch, but... it's just a chore now. I stand there with the hose and I just feel completely flat. There's no joy in it. I don't care if the weeds are taking over the flower beds. I just water them and go right back inside. 

And it's not just the garden, either. It's the same thing with my book club. I've been in this book club with the same group of women for, gosh, almost eight years now. We meet on the second Tuesday of every month. I used to look forward to it for weeks, reading the book, making notes, getting excited to debate the characters over a glass of wine. But the last few months? I barely skim the books, if I even start them at all. I still show up to the meetings because I feel obligated, and I love those women, but I just sit there feeling totally disconnected from the conversation. It all just feels so dull. The last two times, I actually made up an excuse about having an early morning at the hospital just so I could leave an hour early. I just couldn't wait to get out of there and go home, even though once I get home, I don't really want to do anything there either. It's just like the color has been drained out of everything I used to find fun or engaging. I just do it because I'm supposed to, not because I actually want to.
Do you often feel guilty about things?

Guilty? Well... yes, actually. That's something that's been taking up entirely too much space in my head lately. And it's not even about work, which is funny because in my job, if you make a mistake, the consequences are huge. But I know I do my job well. No, it's... it's my personal life. Specifically, my marriage. 

I just... I keep replaying the marriage over and over in my head lately. It's like a movie I can't turn off, just looping these old conversations and arguments and quiet moments where things went wrong. I'll just sit there in the evening and tell myself that I must have failed at something so incredibly basic. Like there was some fundamental rule about being a good partner, or just being a good person to live with, that I completely missed or messed up. I mean, I'm a social worker, for heaven's sake! I literally spend my days helping people navigate communication and family crises, but I couldn't even keep my own marriage intact. 

And the frustrating thing is, the rational, educated part of my brain—the part that went to grad school and understands human behavior—knows perfectly well that relationships are so much more complicated than that. I know it takes two people, I know there's nuance, and I know it's never just one person failing at some basic task that ruins everything. I know all of that logically. But it doesn't stop the guilt. It doesn't stop that heavy, awful feeling in my chest that if I had just been better, or paid more attention, or just been a different kind of wife, maybe it wouldn't have fallen apart. I'll spend hours just agonizing over a passing comment I made five or six years ago, just dissecting it and blaming myself for every little crack in the foundation. It's exhausting, it really is, but I just can't seem to stop putting all the blame squarely on my own shoulders.
Do you often feel anxious or on edge?

Anxious? On edge? No, not really. I mean, I think everyone has a little bit of anxiety these days, just with the state of the world and everything, but no, I wouldn't say I feel anxious or on edge in any significant way. It's funny, because you'd think with the guilt I was just talking about, and the fact that I can't seem to stop replaying everything in my head, that I'd be a nervous wreck. But it's not an anxious feeling. It's more of a... a heavy feeling. A sinking feeling. 

When I think of being anxious, I think of my heart racing, or feeling jittery, or worrying about what's going to happen tomorrow or next week. Like when I first started at the hospital, I used to get so anxious before presenting a complex case to the care team. My palms would sweat, I'd over-prepare, I'd worry they were going to ask me a question I didn't know the answer to. That's anxiety to me. But this? This is entirely different. I don't feel keyed up or nervous about the future. If anything, I feel almost too still. Like I'm just sitting in this heavy, quiet space where I'm just... existing. There's no nervous energy at all. In fact, I'd almost welcome a little nervous energy, just to feel something other than this sort of flat, guilty exhaustion. So, no, I wouldn't use the words anxious or on edge at all. It's just a totally different sensation.
Have you noticed a significant decrease in your interest in activities that you used to find pleasurable?

Well, like I was just saying a few minutes ago about the garden and my book club... yes, absolutely. It's a very significant decrease. I know I probably already talked your ear off about the hydrangeas and the women in my reading group, but that really is the perfect example of what's happening to me right now. 

I still go through the motions of the things I used to absolutely love, like getting out there and watering the flower beds or showing up to the book club on a Tuesday night, but... there's just no spark anymore. Most of the time, it all just feels completely flat. I'll sit there with my friends, looking at them talking and laughing about whatever chapter we were supposed to read, and I just feel like I'm watching them from behind a thick pane of glass. And like I mentioned before, I usually just end up making up some excuse to leave early. Or with the books themselves, I just don't even start reading them at all. 

It's not just that I'm a little bored, it's that the actual drive to participate is just... gone. I used to be the one organizing the book club snacks, you know? I'd bring these elaborate charcuterie boards and print out discussion questions I found online. Now, it takes absolutely everything in me just to walk through my friend's front door and sit on her couch for an hour. So yes, a very significant decrease in my interest. It's like the motivation just completely evaporated, even though I'm still desperately trying to keep up appearances by going through all those old motions.
Have you had any thoughts about not wanting to be alive or wishing you could just disappear?

Well... that's a hard question to answer, honestly. It's... complicated. I mean, first of all, I need to be very clear that I do not have a plan to hurt myself. I know exactly what you're asking, and I know the clinical implications of it, given my background. I don't have a plan, I don't have means, I'm not sitting at home trying to figure out how to end my life. I really need you to know that. 

But... wishing I could just disappear? Or not wanting to be alive? That's... that's where it gets murky. Because, yes, if I'm being completely honest with you, and I suppose that's the whole point of being here... I do sometimes catch myself thinking that it would just be so much easier if I didn't wake up. It usually happens at night, or really early in the morning before the alarm goes off, when that heavy feeling I was telling you about is just pressing down on me so hard. I'll just be lying there in the dark, and this thought will just sort of drift in... this quiet little thought that says, 'Wouldn't it be a relief to just... stop?' To not have to get up and carry all this guilt, and try to force myself to care about the book club or the garden, and just... not have to do it anymore. 

And the thing is, it really scares me when I have those thoughts. It terrifies me, actually. Because I know exactly what I would do if one of my clients at the hospital sat in my office and said those exact words to me. I would take it incredibly seriously. I'd be doing risk assessments, I'd be talking about safety plans, I'd be documenting everything meticulously because I know how dangerous that kind of passive ideation can be. I know the textbook definition of what's happening in my own brain. But when it's me... when it's my own head... it just feels like this overwhelming exhaustion. Like I've been treading water for so long and my arms are just so tired, and the idea of just letting myself sink is... appealing, in a really dark, quiet way. So, no, I'm not going to do anything. But yes, the thoughts are there, and they are frightening precisely because I know better.
How long have you been feeling this way, with the guilt, lack of interest in activities, and thoughts about not wanting to be alive?

Well, it's... it's been a while now. I mean, I can trace it back pretty specifically, which I suppose is a little unusual, but given the circumstances, it makes sense. It all really started after the divorce was finalized. That was... gosh, about a year and seven months ago now. 

And you know, the lead-up to the divorce was stressful, of course it was. It was a long, drawn-out process, lots of mediation, lots of arguing over the house and the assets, and just the emotional toll of unspooling a twenty-year marriage. But during that time, I was running on adrenaline, you know? I was in survival mode. I was still going to work, managing my caseload at the hospital, keeping up with my friends, doing all the things. I was stressed, but I wasn't... this. 

It was only after the ink was dry on the final papers, and he moved the last of his boxes out of the garage, and the house was just... quiet. That's when it hit me. I remember sitting at the kitchen island, looking at the empty space where his coffee mug used to sit, and it was like all the air just rushed out of the room. That's when the guilt started creeping in, all the 'what ifs' and 'if only I had done this differently' thoughts. And then the garden started looking like a chore instead of a sanctuary, and the book club just felt like a massive burden. 

So, yes, a year and seven months. It's been a slow, steady decline since then. At first, I thought it was just normal grief, you know? Adjustment disorder, maybe. I kept telling myself, 'Give it six months, give it a year, you'll bounce back.' But the one-year mark came and went, and instead of bouncing back, I just felt heavier. And then those thoughts about just wanting to disappear started showing up. It's like the longer this goes on, the more entrenched I get in this... this quicksand. So, yeah, nineteen months of this. It feels like a lifetime, honestly.
Have you noticed yourself moving or speaking more slowly than usual?

Moving or speaking more slowly? No, I... I don't think so. I haven't noticed anything like that, and nobody else has pointed it out to me either. 

I mean, as you can probably tell from sitting here with me for the last twenty minutes, I still talk a mile a minute. My friends have always joked that I could talk underwater, and I really don't think my speech has slowed down at all. If anything, because my mind is constantly spinning with all that guilt and all those 'what ifs' I was telling you about, when I finally start talking, it all just sort of spills out of me at my usual rapid-fire pace. I know I'm probably rambling a bit right now, it's just... there's so much to unpack, you know? 

And physically... no, I wouldn't say I'm moving slowly. I'm not walking through molasses or anything like that. It's much more of an internal heaviness rather than a physical slowing down of my actual body. Like, when I'm at the hospital, I'm still walking briskly down the corridors between the wards. I have to, right? The pace of a busy hospital doesn't just pause because one social worker is feeling miserable. Just the other day, actually, I had to get from the oncology wing on the fourth floor all the way down to the ER in the basement for a family in crisis, and I practically sprinted down the stairwell because our staff elevators are always so ridiculously slow. 

So my body works fine. It moves at a completely normal speed once it's in motion. It's just that *getting* the body to start moving, finding the actual will to stand up off the couch and put my shoes on... that takes a monumental amount of mental effort. But once I'm up and doing the thing, my physical pace is exactly the same as it's always been. So, no, no physical slowing down of my movements or my words. Just the... the exhaustion of forcing myself to keep up that normal pace.
Have you noticed any difficulty initiating movements or activities, even if once you start, you can continue at a normal pace?

Yes, exactly. That's exactly it. It's... well, it's just this bone-deep exhaustion that makes starting anything feel like climbing Mount Everest. It’s the fatigue, really. I mean, even on days when my caseload at the hospital is not unusually heavy—like, say it’s a Tuesday and I just have a few routine discharge plans to coordinate, no major traumas, no families in crisis, just standard social work stuff—I still feel like I am literally dragging my body through the hospital. It’s like gravity is turned up to double strength just for me. 

And then... oh gosh, then I get home. I used to have this whole evening routine, you know? I’d come in, I’d cook a proper dinner from scratch, maybe do some stretching in the living room because walking on those hard clinical floors all day really does a number on your lower back, and you have to take care of your body in this profession. But now? Now I walk through the front door and I am just entirely depleted. I am way too tired to even think about getting out a cutting board or chopping a vegetable, so cooking is completely out the window. I definitely don't stretch anymore, my yoga mat has just been gathering dust in the corner for months. 

And my phone... my phone will be buzzing in my purse with personal messages, friends checking in, people from my old circles, and I just... I can't. I am literally too tired to even type out a quick text message to answer them. I just stare at the screen. The thought of initiating even a basic text conversation, of having to summon the energy to sound like my normal self, is just too much. I just leave them unread. So, yes, starting things is incredibly difficult, just because I feel completely and utterly drained of all energy before I even begin.
Do you feel like you have to push yourself to do even small tasks, like getting dressed in the morning?

Getting dressed... oh, getting dressed is a whole ordeal. I do it, because I have to. I mean, I have to go to work. I can't just not show up to the hospital, my patients need me, the care coordinators need me. But the actual process of getting ready? I will sit on the edge of the bed for twenty, maybe thirty minutes just staring at my closet. It’s like I have to mentally negotiate with myself just to pull a pair of slacks off a hanger and put on a blouse. I have to force myself through every single step of the morning routine.

So, yes, I am still getting to work. I haven't called out or taken a leave of absence or anything. But honestly, even though I am physically showing up, I am just barely keeping my head above water once I'm there. My documentation, for example. You know how it is in healthcare, if it's not documented, it didn't happen. The charting is endless—Medicare forms, Medicaid assessments, placement referrals. It used to be second nature to me. I’d just knock out my notes between patient visits or wrap them up right at the end of my shift without a second thought. 

But lately? It is all just backing up. I have piles of files on my desk. I find myself having to stay late, sitting in my office at six-thirty or seven o'clock at night when the rest of the department has already gone home, just trying to fix things and catch up on paperwork that I used to handle so easily. It takes me so much effort to just push through a standard discharge summary now. I have to re-read things, I make silly mistakes I have to go back and correct... it's exhausting. 

And because I am using absolutely every ounce of my willpower just to get dressed, get to the hospital, and struggle through my case notes, there is literally nothing left for anything else. Outside of work, my life has just... well, it's shrunk down to almost nothing. Those basic routines I mentioned before, the cooking, keeping the house tidy, getting the mail... gone. And my friendships, too. Like I said about the text messages, I just let them sit there. And eventually, people stop reaching out when you don't reply, which I suppose is completely fair, but it means my whole social life has basically evaporated. I just don't have the capacity to push myself to do anything beyond the bare minimum required to keep my job, and as I said, even that is starting to slip.
Do you feel like your thoughts are moving slowly, in addition to having trouble starting activities?

Slowly? Yes, actually. It’s... it’s like my brain is wading through wet cement. I was just thinking about this the other day because we have these interdisciplinary case reviews every Wednesday morning, right? The doctors, the charge nurses, the physical therapists, we all sit down in the conference room to go over the complex discharges for the week. I used to just glance at my file and know exactly what to say, I had all the family dynamics and insurance details right there at my fingertips. 

But now? During those case reviews, I find myself having to reread the exact same paragraph of my own notes several times before the words actually register in my brain. It's like I'm looking at the letters, but the meaning just isn't connecting, or it takes forever to process what I myself wrote just a day prior. I just stare at the page trying to force my brain to comprehend it. 

And it's not just the reading, it's... it's the decision-making, too. The processing speed for just basic choices is completely shot. Simple, everyday decisions have become agonizingly slow. For instance, I'll get back to my desk after rounds and have a few voicemails from clients or their families. Before, I'd instantly prioritize them—triage them, basically, like second nature. Now, I will sit there staring at the blinking light on the phone, trying to figure out which client call to return first, and it can take me an embarrassing amount of time just to make that one tiny choice. I just weigh it back and forth, back and forth, and my mind just feels entirely stuck in the mud. 

And it bleeds into my personal life, too, on the rare occasions I actually try to do something normal. Like if I manage to stop at the grocery store on the way home, trying to decide what to buy for dinner... I can stand in the aisle for ten, maybe fifteen minutes just staring at the shelves, completely unable to process what to get. Chicken? Pasta? Soup? It’s like my brain just short-circuits over the most mundane things. It’s ridiculous, I know it's ridiculous because I'm an educated professional who makes life-altering decisions for patients, but right now, just figuring out dinner takes so much time and mental energy that I usually just give up and go home empty-handed. So yes, my thoughts are definitely... they just won't move at their normal speed.
Do you feel like you have difficulty concentrating or making decisions?

Yes, exactly, that's really what I was trying to get at just a moment ago. It's absolutely both of those things—the concentration and the decision-making. 

Like I was just saying about those Wednesday morning case reviews, my concentration is so poor right now that I literally have to sit there in the conference room and reread the exact same paragraph of my own notes several times. And it’s not even complicated medical jargon, you know? It’s my own social work assessments, things I wrote myself, but my eyes just scan over the words and nothing sticks. I have to force myself to focus on every single sentence, almost word by word, just to comprehend what's right in front of me. 

And then with the decisions... yes, it's just like I was telling you. It takes me an absolutely embarrassing amount of time to make even the simplest, most inconsequential choice. Whether it's sitting at my desk trying to figure out which client call to return first, or standing in the middle of the grocery store aisle trying to decide what to buy for dinner... it’s like my brain just completely stalls out. I mean, I have a graduate degree, I've been doing this job for years, I handle complex family dynamics and Medicare regulations all day long, and suddenly I can't even figure out if I should call Mrs. Smith or Mr. Jones first? Or if I should buy chicken or pasta? It’s incredibly frustrating, and honestly, it's quite humiliating when I sort of snap out of it and realize how long I've just been standing there staring blankly at a shelf or my blinking phone. So yes, concentrating on anything or trying to decide anything... both are just completely overwhelming for me right now.
Have you noticed any changes in how you've been feeling over the past few months, either better, worse, or about the same?

Well, the last few months... honestly, it feels like it’s just been one long, continuous stretch of the exact same thing. I wouldn't say it's gotten better, that's for sure. If anything, it's just become more... entrenched? 

But if I really sit back and look at the timeline, it hasn't just been the last few months. This has actually been going on since the divorce was finalized, which was about a year and seven months ago now. I remember the exact timeframe because, you know, when you go through a divorce, you build it up in your head that once the final papers are signed, you're going to feel this profound sense of closure or relief. Like the legal battle is over, the assets are divided, the lawyers are finally paid off, and you can just breathe and start your new life. 

But instead of moving on, that was right around the exact time this absolute wall just hit me. So for the last nineteen months—a year and seven months—it's just been this constant, heavy struggle. Every single month feels exactly like the last one. I kept telling myself, "Oh, next month I'll bounce back, next month I'll get my energy back, next month I'll be back to my old self and I won't be staring blankly at my case files." But here we are, a year and seven months later, and it's just... the same. It's just been sitting with me since the judge signed that decree. It’s a really long time to feel like you're just treading water, waiting to feel normal again.
Do you feel like your body is moving more slowly than usual?

No, actually, I haven't noticed that at all. It's funny you ask, because it's really just the mental part that's the problem. Physically, my body is moving at the exact same pace it always has. 

I mean, working as a social worker in a hospital, you're constantly on your feet, right? I cover two different floors, so I'm always walking back and forth from the ICU down to the general medical wards, up and down the long corridors. And I haven't slowed down physically in the slightest. Just the other day, I had to hustle down to the emergency department because we had a really sudden, tragic trauma case come in, and the charge nurse paged me to come down right away to support the family. I practically sprinted down three flights of stairs because the staff elevators in our building are notoriously slow and I didn't want to keep them waiting. My legs worked perfectly fine, I didn't feel weighed down or anything. 

So my physical ability to just walk, or move my arms, or get up out of a chair... that's all completely normal. I don't feel heavy or sluggish in my limbs whatsoever. It's... it's exactly like I was saying earlier, it's entirely up in my head. The physical vehicle is operating at its normal, everyday speed, but the navigation system—my brain—is just completely shot. So if you're asking if I'm physically moving in slow motion or shuffling around, no, definitely not. Not at all. It's just the thoughts that are stuck.
Do you feel like your movements or reactions are slower than they used to be?

Well, like I was just saying... I feel like you're asking the exact same question again? I really don't feel like my physical movements are slower at all. My reactions, my movements—they're all completely normal. 

I mean, if anything, I'm reacting to things around me just as quickly as I always have. Like I mentioned with that trauma case in the ED, I had to react instantly when that page came through. You don't have time to be slow when a family is in crisis and the medical team needs you there to facilitate. You just drop what you're doing and go. And I did. I didn't hesitate, I didn't stumble, I didn't feel like I was moving through molasses or anything like that. 

Even just driving to work, you know? The traffic on I-95 in the mornings is absolutely brutal, people are constantly cutting you off, and you have to have quick reflexes just to avoid getting into an accident. I haven't noticed any delay in hitting the brakes or swerving if I need to. My body does exactly what it needs to do exactly when it needs to do it. 

It's really just the mental side of things, like I keep trying to explain. The decision-making, the concentrating, the mental fog—that's where everything is bogged down. But physically? No. My reactions and my movements are exactly the same as they were before all of this started. I'm definitely not physically slower.
Do you feel like your body or movements are heavier or more laborious than usual?

I feel like we're just going around in circles here, Doctor. I really don't mean to be difficult, but... it's like you're asking me the exact same thing for a third time, just using slightly different words. No, my body doesn't feel heavier. My movements aren't laborious. 

I don't know how else to explain it. When I think of laborious movements, I think of some of the older patients I see on the general medical floor, the ones who have severe arthritis or who are recovering from major orthopedic surgery, where every single step they take with their walker looks like it takes a monumental amount of physical effort. Or I think of people who have, you know, actual neurological issues where their limbs just won't cooperate. That is absolutely not what I'm experiencing. 

My arms and legs feel exactly the same weight they've always felt. I don't feel like I'm dragging lead weights around my ankles when I walk the halls at the hospital, and I don't feel like my arms are made of concrete when I'm reaching up into the cabinets in the staff breakroom to grab my coffee mug. I'm fifty years old, so sure, maybe I don't pop out of bed with the same physical spring I had when I was twenty-five, but it's not laborious. It's just normal aging. 

The weight I feel is entirely emotional. It's this heavy, suffocating blanket over my mind, not my body. My body is doing its job perfectly fine. I just... I really need you to understand that the physical part of me is intact. It's the mental part that feels completely bogged down and exhausted. So no, no heavy limbs, no laborious movements. Just the same physical me I've always been.
Have you experienced a period of at least two weeks where you felt depressed or lost interest in activities most of the day?

Yes. Yes, definitely. That's... well, that's actually the main reason I finally decided to come in and talk to you. It's been going on for at least two weeks, probably closer to a month if I'm being completely honest with myself. 

It's just this pervasive feeling of... flatness. I don't know how else to describe it. I still try to do the things I usually love, I really do. I try to force myself to just go through the motions, hoping the enjoyment will eventually catch up, you know? Like with my garden. I have this backyard garden that I've spent years cultivating—lots of hydrangeas, hostas, some raised beds for vegetables. Usually, I'd be out there every single evening after my shift at the hospital, pruning and watering and just using that time to decompress from all the heavy stuff I deal with at work. But lately? I go out there with the watering can, and I'm just standing there, and I feel absolutely nothing. It doesn't bring me any peace or joy. It just feels like another chore on a never-ending list. Half the time I don't even start; I just look at the plants, feel completely overwhelmed by the idea of tending to them, and go right back inside.

And it's the exact same thing with my book club. I've been with this same group of women for, gosh, maybe eight years now? We meet once a month, and it's usually the highlight of my week. I still show up, mostly because I don't want to be rude or have them start worrying about me, but I'm just not really *there*. The last time we met, we were supposed to be discussing this historical fiction novel that I normally would have devoured in a single weekend, but I couldn't even bring myself to read past the third chapter. I just sat there on my friend's couch, holding a glass of wine, feeling completely disconnected from the conversation and the laughter. It all just felt so incredibly flat and pointless. I ended up making up an excuse about having an early morning meeting with the hospital discharge planning committee just so I could leave an hour early. 

So, yes. It's like the color has just drained out of everything I used to enjoy. I still try to show up, but I end up leaving early, or I just can't bring myself to start things in the first place. That's exactly what I've been dealing with.
Do you feel like you have difficulty initiating movements or activities, but once you start, you can continue at a normal pace?

I... honestly, Doctor, I feel like I'm repeating myself again. I'm sorry, I know you have to ask these things, but it's like we're just circling the same drain here. No, I don't have trouble initiating movements. It's not like I'm sitting there trying to will my arm to lift and it just won't obey me, or like my legs are glued to the floor when I need to stand up from my desk. 

I mean, just yesterday, I was sitting in my office at the hospital—it's this tiny little windowless room down in the basement, right next to the boiler room, which is a whole other story about how social work is valued, but anyway—I was sitting there, and my pager went off for a consult up on the surgical floor. I didn't sit there struggling to get my body to move. I just stood up, grabbed my clipboard, and walked to the elevator. There was no hesitation, no... no physical barrier to starting the action. 

And it's the same thing at home. If the dog needs to go out, I don't sit on the couch for ten minutes trying to force my body to stand up. I just get up and open the back door. The physical act of starting a movement is perfectly fine. Once I decide to do something, my body does it, and it does it at a completely normal pace from start to finish.

I just... I keep replaying the marriage over and over in my head lately. Like there was some fundamental rule about being a good partner, or just being a good person to live with, that I completely missed or messed up. I mean, I'm a social worker, for heaven's sake! I used to just glance at my file and know exactly what to say, I had all the family dynamics and insurance details right there at my fingertips.

It’s like my brain just short-circuits over the most mundane things. It’s ridiculous, I know it's ridiculous because I'm an educated professional who makes life-altering decisions for patients, but right now, just figuring out dinner takes so much time and mental energy that I usually just give up and go home empty-handed. I mean, I have a graduate degree, I've been doing this job for years, I handle complex family dynamics and Medicare regulations all day long, and suddenly I can't even figure out if I should call Mrs. Smith or Mr. Jones first? Or if I should buy chicken or pasta? It’s incredibly frustrating, and honestly, it's quite humiliating when I sort of snap out of it and realize how long I've just been standing there staring blankly at a shelf or my blinking phone. So yes, concentrating on anything or trying to decide anything... both are just completely overwhelming for me right now.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's condition is improving, worsening, or stable over time
doctor.question: Have you noticed any changes in how you've been feeling over the past few months, either better, worse, or about the same?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been going on since the divorce was finalized, about a year and seven months ago.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the timeline and progression of my symptoms over the past few months, which corresponds to the duration of my condition.

patient.answer:
Well, the last few months... honestly, it feels like it’s just been one long, continuous stretch of the exact same thing. I wouldn't say it's gotten better, that's for sure. If anything, it's just become more... entrenched? 

But if I really sit back and look at the timeline, it hasn't just been the last few months. This has actually been going on since the divorce was finalized, which was about a year and seven months ago now. I remember the exact timeframe because, you know, when you go through a divorce, you build it up in your head that once the final papers are signed, you're going to feel this profound sense of closure or relief. Like the legal battle is over, the assets are divided, the lawyers are finally paid off, and you can just breathe and start your new life. 

But instead of moving on, that was right around the exact time this absolute wall just hit me. So for the last nineteen months—a year and seven months—it's just been this constant, heavy struggle. Every single month feels exactly like the last one. I kept telling myself, "Oh, next month I'll bounce back, next month I'll get my energy back, next month I'll be back to my old self and I won't be staring blankly at my case files." But here we are, a year and seven months later, and it's just... the same. It's just been sitting with me since the judge signed that decree. It’s a really long time to feel like you're just treading water, waiting to feel normal again.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of psychomotor retardation
doctor.question: Do you feel like your body is moving more slowly than usual?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about psychomotor retardation (moving more slowly than usual), which is not included in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
No, actually, I haven't noticed that at all. It's funny you ask, because it's really just the mental part that's the problem. Physically, my body is moving at the exact same pace it always has. 

I mean, working as a social worker in a hospital, you're constantly on your feet, right? I cover two different floors, so I'm always walking back and forth from the ICU down to the general medical wards, up and down the long corridors. And I haven't slowed down physically in the slightest. Just the other day, I had to hustle down to the emergency department because we had a really sudden, tragic trauma case come in, and the charge nurse paged me to come down right away to support the family. I practically sprinted down three flights of stairs because the staff elevators in our building are notoriously slow and I didn't want to keep them waiting. My legs worked perfectly fine, I didn't feel weighed down or anything. 

So my physical ability to just walk, or move my arms, or get up out of a chair... that's all completely normal. I don't feel heavy or sluggish in my limbs whatsoever. It's... it's exactly like I was saying earlier, it's entirely up in my head. The physical vehicle is operating at its normal, everyday speed, but the navigation system—my brain—is just completely shot. So if you're asking if I'm physically moving in slow motion or shuffling around, no, definitely not. Not at all. It's just the thoughts that are stuck.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of psychomotor retardation
doctor.question: Do you feel like your movements or reactions are slower than they used to be?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about psychomotor retardation (slower movements or reactions), which is not included in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Well, like I was just saying... I feel like you're asking the exact same question again? I really don't feel like my physical movements are slower at all. My reactions, my movements—they're all completely normal. 

I mean, if anything, I'm reacting to things around me just as quickly as I always have. Like I mentioned with that trauma case in the ED, I had to react instantly when that page came through. You don't have time to be slow when a family is in crisis and the medical team needs you there to facilitate. You just drop what you're doing and go. And I did. I didn't hesitate, I didn't stumble, I didn't feel like I was moving through molasses or anything like that. 

Even just driving to work, you know? The traffic on I-95 in the mornings is absolutely brutal, people are constantly cutting you off, and you have to have quick reflexes just to avoid getting into an accident. I haven't noticed any delay in hitting the brakes or swerving if I need to. My body does exactly what it needs to do exactly when it needs to do it. 

It's really just the mental side of things, like I keep trying to explain. The decision-making, the concentrating, the mental fog—that's where everything is bogged down. But physically? No. My reactions and my movements are exactly the same as they were before all of this started. I'm definitely not physically slower.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of psychomotor retardation
doctor.question: Do you feel like your body or movements are heavier or more laborious than usual?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about psychomotor retardation (feeling like the body or movements are heavy or laborious), which is not included in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
I feel like we're just going around in circles here, Doctor. I really don't mean to be difficult, but... it's like you're asking me the exact same thing for a third time, just using slightly different words. No, my body doesn't feel heavier. My movements aren't laborious. 

I don't know how else to explain it. When I think of laborious movements, I think of some of the older patients I see on the general medical floor, the ones who have severe arthritis or who are recovering from major orthopedic surgery, where every single step they take with their walker looks like it takes a monumental amount of physical effort. Or I think of people who have, you know, actual neurological issues where their limbs just won't cooperate. That is absolutely not what I'm experiencing. 

My arms and legs feel exactly the same weight they've always felt. I don't feel like I'm dragging lead weights around my ankles when I walk the halls at the hospital, and I don't feel like my arms are made of concrete when I'm reaching up into the cabinets in the staff breakroom to grab my coffee mug. I'm fifty years old, so sure, maybe I don't pop out of bed with the same physical spring I had when I was twenty-five, but it's not laborious. It's just normal aging. 

The weight I feel is entirely emotional. It's this heavy, suffocating blanket over my mind, not my body. My body is doing its job perfectly fine. I just... I really need you to understand that the physical part of me is intact. It's the mental part that feels completely bogged down and exhausted. So no, no heavy limbs, no laborious movements. Just the same physical me I've always been.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's condition meets the criteria for a major depressive episode
doctor.question: Have you experienced a period of at least two weeks where you felt depressed or lost interest in activities most of the day?

target_item.name: Loss_of_Interest
target_item.manifestation: I still go through the motions of things I used to love, like watering the garden or showing up to book club, but most of the time it feels flat and I end up leaving early or not starting at all.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if I have experienced a period of at least two weeks where I felt depressed or lost interest in activities most of the day, which directly corresponds to the Loss of Interest symptom.

patient.answer:
Yes. Yes, definitely. That's... well, that's actually the main reason I finally decided to come in and talk to you. It's been going on for at least two weeks, probably closer to a month if I'm being completely honest with myself. 

It's just this pervasive feeling of... flatness. I don't know how else to describe it. I still try to do the things I usually love, I really do. I try to force myself to just go through the motions, hoping the enjoyment will eventually catch up, you know? Like with my garden. I have this backyard garden that I've spent years cultivating—lots of hydrangeas, hostas, some raised beds for vegetables. Usually, I'd be out there every single evening after my shift at the hospital, pruning and watering and just using that time to decompress from all the heavy stuff I deal with at work. But lately? I go out there with the watering can, and I'm just standing there, and I feel absolutely nothing. It doesn't bring me any peace or joy. It just feels like another chore on a never-ending list. Half the time I don't even start; I just look at the plants, feel completely overwhelmed by the idea of tending to them, and go right back inside.

And it's the exact same thing with my book club. I've been with this same group of women for, gosh, maybe eight years now? We meet once a month, and it's usually the highlight of my week. I still show up, mostly because I don't want to be rude or have them start worrying about me, but I'm just not really *there*. The last time we met, we were supposed to be discussing this historical fiction novel that I normally would have devoured in a single weekend, but I couldn't even bring myself to read past the third chapter. I just sat there on my friend's couch, holding a glass of wine, feeling completely disconnected from the conversation and the laughter. It all just felt so incredibly flat and pointless. I ended up making up an excuse about having an early morning meeting with the hospital discharge planning committee just so I could leave an hour early. 

So, yes. It's like the color has just drained out of everything I used to enjoy. I still try to show up, but I end up leaving early, or I just can't bring myself to start things in the first place. That's exactly what I've been dealing with.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of psychomotor retardation
doctor.question: Do you feel like you have difficulty initiating movements or activities, but once you start, you can continue at a normal pace?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about difficulty initiating movements, which is a symptom of psychomotor retardation. This is not included in the patient's symptom profile.

patient.answer:
I... honestly, Doctor, I feel like I'm repeating myself again. I'm sorry, I know you have to ask these things, but it's like we're just circling the same drain here. No, I don't have trouble initiating movements. It's not like I'm sitting there trying to will my arm to lift and it just won't obey me, or like my legs are glued to the floor when I need to stand up from my desk. 

I mean, just yesterday, I was sitting in my office at the hospital—it's this tiny little windowless room down in the basement, right next to the boiler room, which is a whole other story about how social work is valued, but anyway—I was sitting there, and my pager went off for a consult up on the surgical floor. I didn't sit there struggling to get my body to move. I just stood up, grabbed my clipboard, and walked to the elevator. There was no hesitation, no... no physical barrier to starting the action. 

And it's the same thing at home. If the dog needs to go out, I don't sit on the couch for ten minutes trying to force my body to stand up. I just get up and open the back door. The physical act of starting a movement is perfectly fine. Once I decide to do something, my body does it, and it does it at a completely normal pace from start to finish. 

The problem, like I keep saying, isn't my body. It's not my muscles or my motor skills or whatever you want to call it. It's the mental exhaustion. It's the feeling of not *wanting* to do the activity in the first place because everything feels so pointless and flat. But if you're asking specifically about the physical ability to initiate a movement? No. I don't have any trouble with that at all. My body works just fine. It's just... it's everything else that's the problem.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of psychomotor retardation
doctor.question: Do you feel like you're moving more slowly physically than you used to?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about psychomotor retardation (moving more slowly physically), which is not included in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Doctor, I... I really, truly do not mean to be difficult, but I feel like I'm losing my mind a little bit here with these questions. Are you... are you asking me the exact same thing again? Because I feel like I just answered this when you asked about the heaviness and the trouble starting things. 

No. I am not moving more slowly physically. Not at all. Like I've been trying to say, my actual, physical body is operating at the exact same speed it always has. 

I mean, just to give you a picture of my day, when I'm at the hospital, I am constantly on the go. If I get paged to the ER down on the first floor because there's a family in crisis, and I'm all the way up on the oncology ward on the fourth floor, I am speed-walking down those halls. I'm dodging the linen carts, I'm weaving around the food service trays, I'm keeping pace with the medical residents who are half my age. I don't feel like I'm moving through molasses. I don't look like someone who is playing in slow motion. My colleagues haven't been asking me if I hurt my leg or if I'm feeling sick because I'm lagging behind them in the corridors. 

My physical speed is completely, one hundred percent normal. It's just... it's the mental energy that's gone. The joy is gone, like I talked about with my garden and the book club. But if I need to get from point A to point B, my legs carry me there just as fast as they did a year ago, or five years ago for that matter. 

So, no, absolutely no physical slowness. I really, really hope we can move past the physical stuff now, because I just don't know how many more ways I can explain that my body is perfectly fine.
